In the printed tradition, are the accents of the Decalogue grammatical?

The question

Each Decalogue — the one in Exodus and the one in Deuteronomy — has two strands of cantillation, the טעם תחתון and the טעם עליון; in truth there are four, because at the opening commandment the printed tradition (p-trad) differs from the manuscript tradition (m-trad), yielding two different עליון strands and two different תחתון strands. Richard Goerwitz's accent grammar checker vets the manuscript tradition's cantillation as grammatical prose; this page asks the companion question for the printed tradition (still visible in more traditional editions like Koren and Simanim): fed through the same grammar checker, are its תחתון and עליון accentuations grammatical too?

There is no dual cantillation to detangle here. Where the Tiberian manuscript packs both of its strands into one text, the Wikisource base page עשרת הדברות בסיס/טעמים spells out all the strands — printed and manuscript alike — separately and word-for-word, each as plain single cantillation. Every chanted verse (delimited by its own sof pasuq) is grammar-checked on its own. The manuscript tradition is the baseline — MAM's own authoritative text, expected to parse clean throughout — and the printed tradition is the object of study.

The verdict

Manuscript traditionPrinted tradition
Exodus 20 — taḥton✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Exodus 20 — elyon✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)
Deuteronomy 5 — taḥton✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Deuteronomy 5 — elyon✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)

תחתון is grammatical everywhere — both books, both traditions. The printed תחתון differs from the manuscript only in details that do not touch the accent grammar (vocalization such as תִּרְצַח vs תִּרְצָח at לא תרצח, and where a maqaf or ga‘ya falls), and in one verse boundary: the printed תחתון ends its first verse at מבית עבדים (so it has one more verse than the manuscript, which runs the first two commandments together). Both parse clean.

עליון is grammatical in the manuscript but not in the printed tradition: the printed עליון of each Decalogue has exactly one ungrammatical chanted verse — its opening one.

The four strands of אנכי…עבדים

The manuscript and printed traditions accent the Decalogue's אנכי…עבדים unit differently. The accent on עבדים is what decides the structure: a silluq + sof pasuq there ends the verse, so אנכי…עבדים stands as its own verse; an etnaḥta or revia there is mid-verse, folding אנכי…עבדים into a longer verse. The table below lays all four strands over the same milestone columns — אנכי (their common start), then עבדים, על־פני, and מצותי — so their subset relation is plain: every verse starts green at אנכי and ends red at its own last word, the shorter ones stopping where the longer ones keep going. Each strand keeps its own accent on עבדים, the structure-deciding mark (the column ordering is schematic — it shows only which endpoint comes before which, not the real distances between them):

mTאנכי֙עבד֑יםעל־פנֽי׃
mE/pTאנכ֖יעבדֽים׃
pEאנכי֙עבד֗יםעל־פנ֗ימצותֽי׃

How many chanted verses each strand divides the Exodus Decalogue into:

strandchanted verses (Exodus)
m-trad תחתון12
m-trad עליון10
p-trad תחתון13
p-trad עליון9
  • Printed תחתון = manuscript עליון. Once אנכי…עבדים is its own verse there is only one grammatical way to accent it — etnaḥta in the middle, silluq at the end — so both traditions land on the same marks (consonants, accents, and accent-boundary marks: sof pasuq, maqaf, legarmeh). They differ only by an immaterial meteg (which the stripped cells above drop), so the table gives them a single shared row, labelled mE/pT.
  • Printed עליון ≠ manuscript עליון. The printed עליון puts revia on עבדים and runs the first two commandments together into one verse (→ 9 total), where the manuscript עליון closes on silluq (→ 10).
  • The manuscript תחתון does not give אנכי…עבדים its own verse either — it runs אנכי…פני together (etnaḥta at עבדים, sof pasuq at פני), a third structure again.

Only one of these four strands is ungrammatical — the printed עליון, whose merged opening verse the section below dissects.

Why the printed עליון fails: the merged first verse

In the manuscript עליון, the first commandment אָנֹכִי … עֲבָדִים is its own chanted verse, and לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים begins the next — two separate verses, both of which parse clean. The printed tradition instead merges the first two commandments into a single verse (nine chanted verses in all, against the manuscript’s ten). That one merged verse is what the grammar rejects. Shown stripped to consonants and accents (MAM-simple style) and divided at the printed תחתון’s verse boundaries — one עליון verse (E) spanning the five ordinary תחתון verses (T) it merges:

Eאנכי֙…מצותֽי׃
Tאנכ֖י…עבדֽים׃לא־יהי֥ה…על־פנֽי׃לא־תעש֨ה…לאֽרץ׃לא־תשתחו֥ה…לשנאֽי׃וע֥שה…מצותֽי׃
e
t

The single etnaḥta falls at לְשֹׂנְאָי, leaving an over-long first half that has a segolta plus three separate revia domains (at עֲבָדִים, עַל־פָּנַי, and לָאָרֶץ); the prose grammar cannot build it and returns a pashta_phrase error — the same failure, at the same structural point, in both Decalogues.

The cause is the merged structure, not sheer length: Deuteronomy’s printed עליון Sabbath verse runs 55 words and parses clean, while this merged verse (51 words) does not. Keeping the two commandments as the manuscript’s two separate verses (9 and 42 words) is exactly what lets them parse.
